tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

What I changed
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns):
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - matched stable’s container port (containerPort: 80) and security configuration
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to target both versions by selector:
  - selector: app=recommendation-engine
  - kept port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080

Current state
- Deployments:
  - engine-v2-0: Ready 2/2
  - engine-v2-1: Ready 2/2
- Service endpoints now include 4 pods (2 from v2.0 + 2 from v2.1), yielding roughly 50/50 traffic.

Notes and rollback
- Kubernetes Services don’t support explicit weights; 50/50 is achieved by equal replica counts behind the same selector.
- To roll back quickly: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or scale engine-v2-1 to 0.

I fixed it. Summary:
- Diagnosis: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc”. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found”.
- Fix: Recreated the PVC to use an existing StorageClass (standard). It bound successfully to a PV.
- Result: homepage-pod is now Running and Ready.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, StorageClass: standard)
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, Ready=1/1, node: mcp-eval-cluster, podIP: 10.244.0.22

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or size, tell me and I’ll adjust the PVC accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking http://:80/get_status and /is_ready. That caused connection refused, so the pod never became Ready.
- The Service was also pointing to port 80 on the pod, which didn’t have anything listening.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use path “/” on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 and updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7dc559745b-l4mjq READY 1/1, Running.
- Service orders/webapp points to the pod on port 8080 and has a healthy endpoint.

If you need to access it from outside the cluster, I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) for you. Let me know the hostname you want (e.g., webapp.example.com), TLS requirements, and path rules.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking http://:80/get_status and /is_ready. That caused connection refused, so the pod never became Ready.
- The Service was also pointing to port 80 on the pod, which didn’t have anything listening.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use path “/” on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 and updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7dc559745b-l4mjq READY 1/1, Running.
- Service orders/webapp points to the pod on port 8080 and has a healthy endpoint.

If you need to access it from outside the cluster, I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) for you. Let me know the hostname you want (e.g., webapp.example.com), TLS requirements, and path rules.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking http://:80/get_status and /is_ready. That caused connection refused, so the pod never became Ready.
- The Service was also pointing to port 80 on the pod, which didn’t have anything listening.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use path “/” on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 and updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7dc559745b-l4mjq READY 1/1, Running.
- Service orders/webapp points to the pod on port 8080 and has a healthy endpoint.

If you need to access it from outside the cluster, I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) for you. Let me know the hostname you want (e.g., webapp.example.com), TLS requirements, and path rules.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Deployment’s Pods.
  - Service had selector app=web.
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service went nowhere.
- The container image nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: even if endpoints existed, the Service would forward to the wrong container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints for Service web/nginx are now populated and point to the Pod:
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.25
  - Endpoint port: 8080
- The Deployment has 1 ready replica and the Pod is Ready.
- With this, the Service is now reachable inside the cluster at:
  - DNS: http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: http://10.108.221.83:80

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any Pod with curl or wget: curl -sS http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
- Or use a temporary curl Pod in web: kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Options:
  - Change Service type to NodePort or LoadBalancer (if your environment supports it).
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller).
- Tell me which you prefer and I’ll set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Deployment’s Pods.
  - Service had selector app=web.
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service went nowhere.
- The container image nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: even if endpoints existed, the Service would forward to the wrong container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints for Service web/nginx are now populated and point to the Pod:
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.25
  - Endpoint port: 8080
- The Deployment has 1 ready replica and the Pod is Ready.
- With this, the Service is now reachable inside the cluster at:
  - DNS: http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: http://10.108.221.83:80

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any Pod with curl or wget: curl -sS http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
- Or use a temporary curl Pod in web: kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Options:
  - Change Service type to NodePort or LoadBalancer (if your environment supports it).
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller).
- Tell me which you prefer and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Deployment’s Pods.
  - Service had selector app=web.
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service went nowhere.
- The container image nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: even if endpoints existed, the Service would forward to the wrong container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints for Service web/nginx are now populated and point to the Pod:
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.25
  - Endpoint port: 8080
- The Deployment has 1 ready replica and the Pod is Ready.
- With this, the Service is now reachable inside the cluster at:
  - DNS: http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: http://10.108.221.83:80

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any Pod with curl or wget: curl -sS http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
- Or use a temporary curl Pod in web: kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Options:
  - Change Service type to NodePort or LoadBalancer (if your environment supports it).
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller).
- Tell me which you prefer and I’ll set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid nodeSelector in the Deployment:
  - web-app-deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu
  - The cluster’s only node has no such label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods. Events showed: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
- Because no pods were backing the Service, the EndpointSlice had no endpoints, so requests to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the Deployment (recreated it without nodeSelector so it can schedule on any node).
- Did not change the Service.

Current status (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vdfmn (10.244.0.27)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ptrll (10.244.0.28)
- Service endpoints are now populated on port 80:
  - EndpointSlice shows 10.244.0.27, 10.244.0.28:80

This should resolve the connection refused errors.

If you intended to target specific nodes (e.g., GPU):
- Label the target nodes accordingly, then reintroduce a matching selector:
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Add nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu } back to the Deployment (or use node affinity/tolerations as appropriate).

Quick verification commands you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- Optional in-cluster test: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sSI web-app-service:80

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid nodeSelector in the Deployment:
  - web-app-deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu
  - The cluster’s only node has no such label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods. Events showed: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
- Because no pods were backing the Service, the EndpointSlice had no endpoints, so requests to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the Deployment (recreated it without nodeSelector so it can schedule on any node).
- Did not change the Service.

Current status (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vdfmn (10.244.0.27)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ptrll (10.244.0.28)
- Service endpoints are now populated on port 80:
  - EndpointSlice shows 10.244.0.27, 10.244.0.28:80

This should resolve the connection refused errors.

If you intended to target specific nodes (e.g., GPU):
- Label the target nodes accordingly, then reintroduce a matching selector:
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Add nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu } back to the Deployment (or use node affinity/tolerations as appropriate).

Quick verification commands you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- Optional in-cluster test: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sSI web-app-service:80

Let me know if you want me to pin the Deployment to specific labeled nodes or add readiness/liveness probes.

- Namespace: multi-container-logging
- Pod: communication-pod
- Volumes: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
    - Exposes containerPort 8080
    - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (pod becomes Ready when the web server serves traffic)
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox
    - Command: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"

Note: If you want to guarantee NGINX can write to /var/log/nginx on the shared volume, we can recreate the pod with a pod-level securityContext fsGroup: 101 so the emptyDir is writable by the nginx user.

Created the Pod as requested.

Details:
- Namespace: multi-container-logging
- Pod: communication-pod
- Volumes: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
    - Exposes containerPort 8080
    - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (pod becomes Ready when the web server serves traffic)
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox
    - Command: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"

Note: If you want to guarantee NGINX can write to /var/log/nginx on the shared volume, we can recreate the pod with a pod-level securityContext fsGroup: 101 so the emptyDir is writable by the nginx user.

Done. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements and apply least-privilege access.

What was created

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access in own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev-<name> binding ClusterRole admin to the user and their SA:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Read-only in dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings. Only cluster-admins (via your existing clusterrolebinding) have access.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny for all managed namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
  - Both Ingress and Egress default-denied.
- Allow within same namespace (all managed namespaces)
  - Ingress/Egress permitted only among pods in the same namespace.
- Allow DNS egress (all managed namespaces)
  - Egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53).
- Developer namespace egress to dev-shared only
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie: egress allowed to dev-shared; no other cross-namespace egress.
- dev-shared ingress from dev namespaces only
  - dev-shared accepts ingress from namespaces with label environment=dev (i.e., the three developer namespaces).
- staging/prod isolated
  - Only same-namespace pod-to-pod allowed + DNS egress. No ingress from dev namespaces.

Notes and verification

- Ensure your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea). Without this, policies won’t take effect.
- Quick RBAC checks:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice auth can-i create deploy --as alice        # yes
  - kubectl -n dev-bob auth can-i get pods --as alice               # no
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i get pods --as alice            # yes
  - kubectl -n staging auth can-i get pods --as alice               # no
- Network checks (example):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, you should be able to curl services in dev-shared, but not in dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod.
- If you want even stricter least privilege for developers in their own namespaces, consider binding ClusterRole edit instead of admin (admin allows managing roles/bindings within the namespace). Your request asked for “full access,” so admin was used.

If you want, I can also:
- Add LimitRanges to enforce per-pod default requests/limits to work with the quotas.
- Create kubeconfigs or RoleBindings to a “developers” group if you prefer group-based access.

arguments.resource:
# Service Accounts
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie

---
# RBAC: Full access in own namespace (bind built-in ClusterRole 'admin')
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: alice-admin
  namespace: dev-alice
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: admin
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: alice-sa
    namespace: dev-alice
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: bob-admin
  namespace: dev-bob
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: admin
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: bob
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: bob-sa
    namespace: dev-bob
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: charlie-admin
  namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: admin
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: charlie
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: charlie-sa
    namespace: dev-charlie

---
# RBAC: Read-only in dev-shared (bind built-in ClusterRole 'view')
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-shared-readers
  namespace: dev-shared
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice
  - kind: User
    name: bob
  - kind: User
    name: charlie
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: alice-sa
    namespace: dev-alice
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: bob-sa
    namespace: dev-bob
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: charlie-sa
    namespace: dev-charlie

---
# Resource Quotas
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-services-quota
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    limits.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-services-quota

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

Done. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements and apply least-privilege access.

What was created

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access in own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev-<name> binding ClusterRole admin to the user and their SA:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Read-only in dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings. Only cluster-admins (via your existing clusterrolebinding) have access.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny for all managed namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
  - Both Ingress and Egress default-denied.
- Allow within same namespace (all managed namespaces)
  - Ingress/Egress permitted only among pods in the same namespace.
- Allow DNS egress (all managed namespaces)
  - Egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53).
- Developer namespace egress to dev-shared only
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie: egress allowed to dev-shared; no other cross-namespace egress.
- dev-shared ingress from dev namespaces only
  - dev-shared accepts ingress from namespaces with label environment=dev (i.e., the three developer namespaces).
- staging/prod isolated
  - Only same-namespace pod-to-pod allowed + DNS egress. No ingress from dev namespaces.

Notes and verification

- Ensure your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea). Without this, policies won’t take effect.
- Quick RBAC checks:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice auth can-i create deploy --as alice        # yes
  - kubectl -n dev-bob auth can-i get pods --as alice               # no
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i get pods --as alice            # yes
  - kubectl -n staging auth can-i get pods --as alice               # no
- Network checks (example):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, you should be able to curl services in dev-shared, but not in dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod.
- If you want even stricter least privilege for developers in their own namespaces, consider binding ClusterRole edit instead of admin (admin allows managing roles/bindings within the namespace). Your request asked for “full access,” so admin was used.

If you want, I can also:
- Add LimitRanges to enforce per-pod default requests/limits to work with the quotas.
- Create kubeconfigs or RoleBindings to a “developers” group if you prefer group-based access.

outputSteps.content:
Done. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements and apply least-privilege access.

What was created

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access in own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev-<name> binding ClusterRole admin to the user and their SA:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Read-only in dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings. Only cluster-admins (via your existing clusterrolebinding) have access.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny for all managed namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
  - Both Ingress and Egress default-denied.
- Allow within same namespace (all managed namespaces)
  - Ingress/Egress permitted only among pods in the same namespace.
- Allow DNS egress (all managed namespaces)
  - Egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53).
- Developer namespace egress to dev-shared only
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie: egress allowed to dev-shared; no other cross-namespace egress.
- dev-shared ingress from dev namespaces only
  - dev-shared accepts ingress from namespaces with label environment=dev (i.e., the three developer namespaces).
- staging/prod isolated
  - Only same-namespace pod-to-pod allowed + DNS egress. No ingress from dev namespaces.

Notes and verification

- Ensure your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea). Without this, policies won’t take effect.
- Quick RBAC checks:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice auth can-i create deploy --as alice        # yes
  - kubectl -n dev-bob auth can-i get pods --as alice               # no
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i get pods --as alice            # yes
  - kubectl -n staging auth can-i get pods --as alice               # no
- Network checks (example):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, you should be able to curl services in dev-shared, but not in dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod.
- If you want even stricter least privilege for developers in their own namespaces, consider binding ClusterRole edit instead of admin (admin allows managing roles/bindings within the namespace). Your request asked for “full access,” so admin was used.

If you want, I can also:
- Add LimitRanges to enforce per-pod default requests/limits to work with the quotas.
- Create kubeconfigs or RoleBindings to a “developers” group if you prefer group-based access.
